name: Church and State: the 'divine nation'
plain_explanation: Early Christians were taught they should not take part in running the (pagan) state, but should focus their political loyalty on the Church, the 'divine nation' -- a stance that shaped how the Church related to secular power ever afterward.
precise_definition: Origen's doctrine that Christians should not participate in the government of the (pagan) State but only of the 'divine nation,' i.e., the Church -- a doctrine later modified after Constantine but never wholly abandoned, and, Russell argues, implicit in Saint Augustine's later City of God.
why_it_mattered: It encouraged churchmen to treat secular political collapse (e.g., the fall of Rome) as relatively unimportant compared to Church affairs, while channeling their formidable talents into Church discipline, theology, and monastic expansion.
historical_origin: Formulated by Origen in Against Celsus.
examples: Churchmen's relative passivity toward secular administrative decay during the fall of the Western Empire, discussed further in Chapter III
influence_on_later_thinkers: A direct forerunner of Saint Augustine's City of God (Chapter IV) and of the broader medieval dualism of Church and State that structures the rest of Book Two.
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Central to Christian political theology from this point forward.
